text.p: The main stories in the Austrian press this Tuesday are:
DIE PRESSE
- As the government plans to make early retirement much less attractive, figures show that one thousand more early pensions were taken out in June than in May.
- Chancellor Viktor Klima (SPOe) and his conservatiove People's Party coalition partner Wolfgang Schuessel are both on holiday for two weeks. Klima is in the Malaysian jungle, Schuessel in America.
- Troubled conservative People's Party leader Wolfgang Schuessel says that despite his party's plummeting poll performance he sees no need for any personnel or policy changes.
- The Bank Austria/Creditanstalt (BA/CA) group revealed its half-year results on Monday. It recorded higher profits and said and said it saw room for higher dividends.
- Milk is to become one schilling more expensive per liter from August, but whether this is passsed on to customers depends on what the retail chains do.
- Banks Erste and GiroCredit, which fused together in January, presented their last independent half year balances on Monday. There was a small profit increase.

- Barbara Schenk is to replace Bernhard Chytra as manager of the Austrian unit of electronics firm Grundig. The change has nothing to do with a dispute over the separation of Grundig and Phillips, a statement said.

- Germany pips Austria to the first place post in Europe's leauge table of fruit juice consumption. Austrians drank 33 litres per head in 1996, taking second place behind Germany at 41.1 litres per head.
DER STANDARD
- "Road pricing for private cars is dead", says SPOe whip Peter Kostelka.
- Government, employer and union representatives will meet every Monday morning in August to discuss pension reform and come up with solutions upon which everyone can agree.
- The conservative Poeple's Party presented its plans for the forthcoming elections to the Upper Austrian state parliament on Monday. The elections are due to take place in October.
KURIER
- Back pains are Austria's number one illness: some 85 percent of the population has had back problems at least once in their life.
- The opposition welcomes changing views in the Social Democrats over compulsory military service.

- Austria and Germany no longer want to be the paymasters of the EU. Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel says there should be more justice in EU contributions and will use Austria's EU presidency in the second half of 1998 to achieve this.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN
- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlingher has told the provinces to keep their new borrowing in 1998 at a maximum 0.2 percent. The new savings aim to make sure Austria qualifies for EMU.
- Creditanstalt has accepted an improved bid from Ernst Alexander Maier and Mirko Kovats for Emco.
- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger says he does not want to push through pension reform against union wishes.
- Bank Austria is expecting to reach a solution in its dispute with HTM this week.
WIENER ZEITUNG
- Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is to make an official visit to Vienna in September at the invitation of Chancellor Viktor Klima.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- Privatisation of OKA wobbles: the EVN Consortium's 5.1 billion schilling offer demands too many rights and this goes against the invitation of tenders.
- The listed dairy company NOeM has converted all preference shares into ordinary shares and has thus fundamentally altered the voting right relationship.
